name: rrdtool
why: A round-robin time-series database with a fixed-size circular store; an old-school idea that still quietly underpins monitoring graphs.

brief.what_it_is: RRDtool is a data logging and graphing system for time series data, which the homepage calls "the OpenSource industry standard" for this job. It stores values in round robin databases: files created at a fixed size and pre-filled with UNKNOWN data, whose archives wrap around as new data arrives. Timestamped values go in through rrdupdate or rrdtool create and related commands, and the tool can give back fetched data, XML dumps, and graphs. The homepage says it can be called from shell scripts and from perl, python, ruby, lua or tcl applications.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents it as a high-performance system for logging and graphing time series data that can be embedded in ordinary scripts and applications. The fixed-size design is my inference from the docs rather than the author's stated reason: files are created at their final full size, so storage stays bounded.
brief.how_it_works: Each RRD defines one or more data sources (DS) at create time, each with a type such as GAUGE, COUNTER, DERIVE or ABSOLUTE, plus a heartbeat and optional min and max. Updates arriving at arbitrary times are folded into primary data points on each step interval, and round robin archives (RRA) consolidate those with AVERAGE, MIN, MAX or LAST into a fixed number of rows that wrap around. Counter-type sources are stored as per-second rates, not running totals.

commands_seen.cmd: rrdtool create filename [--start|-b start time] [--step|-s step] [--template|-t template-file] [--source|-r source-file] [--no-overwrite|-O] [--daemon|-d address] [DS:ds-name[=mapped-ds-name[[source-index]]]:DST:dst arguments] [RRA:CF:cf arguments]

Doc example: sets up an RRD that accepts one temperature value every 300 seconds, followed by a DS line and four RRA lines.
Creates a file through a running rrdcached daemon over a Unix socket instead of writing directly. The I<> is literal text left in the doc.
Doc example opening line for a file collecting power values once per second, with the scaled-duration form (--step 1s, RRA durations like 10d) shown in the same section.

brief.install_notes: The homepage says RRDtool is downloadable from the site, compiles on a number of Linux and Unix platforms, and also builds on Microsoft Windows. It describes an rrdbuild documentation page with build instructions, which I did not fetch. Nothing I read mentions accounts, runtimes or first-run configuration. The executables list includes rrdcached, a data caching daemon, and rrdcgi, which builds web pages from RRD graph templates.
brief.standout: The fixed-size circular store means the file never grows, and the rrdcreate doc is unusually frank about trade-offs, such as COUNTER versus DERIVE and how a counter reset can be mistaken for a wrap. It also ships built-in Holt-Winters forecasting and failure flagging (HWPREDICT, FAILURES) and COMPUTE data sources that act like virtual columns.
brief.status: unknown. The homepage news pointer is dated 02/20/2017, the docs index 10/24/2012, and the rrdcreate page 02/04/2019. I did not check a release page or repository, so I cannot say whether it is actively maintained.
brief.caveats: The homepage is mostly navigation and boilerplate, so the substance came from the docs pages. I did not reach a GitHub README or confirm the version the docs describe. Prefilling from source files is best-effort with no guarantee of correctness. Holt-Winters features need a matched set of RRAs to work. New RRD files get mode 0644 regardless of umask. The homepage's download text claims Windows support, which I did not verify.

judge.reason: Its fixed-size circular time-series store and built-in consolidation and forecasting make this more than another graphing tool, and it remains unfamiliar to many developers.

entry.title: rrdtool
entry.tldr: A time-series database whose files are created at full size and wrap around like a ring buffer, so a decade of graphs never outgrows its disk space.
entry.deeper_look:
RRDtool logs numbers over time and draws graphs from them. You define a database up front: one or more data sources (each a GAUGE, COUNTER, DERIVE or ABSOLUTE, with a heartbeat and optional min and max) and a set of round robin archives. The file is created at its final size and pre-filled with UNKNOWN. New values overwrite the oldest ones as the archives wrap, so storage stays bounded.

Updates can arrive at irregular times. RRDtool folds them into primary data points on each step interval, then consolidates those into archives using AVERAGE, MIN, MAX or LAST. You might keep fine-grained recent data and coarser data for older periods, all in one file. Counter-type sources are stored as per-second rates, not running totals. In the project's words: "RRDtool stores rates in amount/second for COUNTER, DERIVE, DCOUNTER, DDERIVE and ABSOLUTE data."

The idea underneath is that monitoring data has a natural decay. You want detail about now and a summary of last year, and you do not want to manage retention jobs. Deciding that at create time makes the database a fixed-size object you can reason about. The rrdcreate docs are frank about the trade-offs, such as COUNTER versus DERIVE and how a counter reset can be mistaken for a wrap.

There is more inside. It has built-in Holt-Winters forecasting and failure flagging (HWPREDICT, FAILURES), and COMPUTE data sources that act like virtual columns. The install also includes rrdcached, a caching daemon for batching writes, and rrdcgi, which builds web pages from graph templates. The homepage says it can be called from shell scripts and from perl, python, ruby, lua or tcl.

Starts the doc example for a file collecting power values once per second. The docs show the scaled-duration form there, such as --step 1s and RRA durations like 10d.

entry.whats_unique: The database never grows, because old data is overwritten by design. It also ships forecasting with Holt-Winters and graphing in the same tool.
entry.caveats: Maintenance status is unclear from the pages read (docs are dated between 2012 and 2019), and the Holt-Winters features need a matched set of RRAs to work.
